title: Distance-Hiding Fingerprints for Text Embeddings via Secure SimHash

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The purpose of the contribution is to characterize the privacy leakage in binary LSH fingerprints. None of the prior papers explicitly address this specific purpose. While several papers discuss privacy leakage in general (e.g., [1], [2], [3], [6], [9], [11]), they do not focus on binary LSH fingerprints or provide a characterization of privacy leakage specific to this context. For example, [1] discusses lightweight private similarity search but does not analyze privacy leakage in binary LSH fingerprints. Similarly, [9] focuses on privacy-preserving Hamming distance computation but does not characterize privacy leakage in binary LSH fingerprints. Therefore, no prior paper covers this purpose.

### Mechanism
The mechanism formalizes the privacy-utility tradeoff for binary fingerprints and identifies the SimHash collision probability curve \(P(s) = (1+s)/2\) as the root cause of pairwise-distance leakage. Paper [15] discusses the collision probability of SimHash and compares it to MinHash, providing a theoretical analysis of SimHash's behavior. While [15] does not explicitly frame this as a privacy-utility tradeoff or link it to pairwise-distance leakage, the underlying primitive of analyzing the SimHash collision probability curve is present. Thus, the mechanism is covered by [15].

### Evaluation
The evaluation is an analytical characterization with no numeric metric, focusing on framing and formalization. Analytical characterizations of privacy-utility tradeoffs appear in prior work, such as [7], [12], and [14]. For example, [7] quantifies privacy-utility tradeoffs in differential privacy, and [14] investigates the tradeoff between privacy and utility using mutual information. While these papers do not analyze binary LSH fingerprints specifically, the evaluation design — analytical characterization of privacy-utility tradeoffs — is covered by these prior works.

### Domain
The domain is privacy-preserving similarity search over text-embedding fingerprints. This domain is well-covered by prior work, including [1], [2], [3], [6], [9], and [11], which all address privacy-preserving similarity search in various forms. For example, [1] and [6] focus on private similarity search, while [9] and [11] address privacy-preserving Hamming distance computation and similarity-based search over encrypted data, respectively. Although the specific focus on binary LSH fingerprints is new, the general application area of privacy-preserving similarity search is covered.

This purpose is about creating a transformation of data fingerprints such that similarity/distance information is hidden from an adversary while still allowing near-neighbor detection. Paper [3] "Sub-Linear Privacy-Preserving Near-Neighbor Search" also targets this objective. The core objective — hide distance information while preserving near-neighbor utility — is covered by [1], [3], and [15].

## MECHANISM: "Secure SimHash composes k independent SimHash bits with XOR so collision probability becomes P_sec(s)=1/2+1/2*p(s)^k, flattening curves for non-neighbors while preserving near-neighbor detection"

The specific mechanism is: take k SimHash bits, XOR-compose them, producing a new collision probability formula that pushes low-similarity pairs toward 0.5 while keeping high-similarity pairs detectable. Paper [8] discusses LSH with k hash functions to "achieve more desirable collision curves" — it analyzes how composing k hash functions changes collision probability curves, which is the same primitive. However, [8] uses AND/OR composition for amplification, not XOR for flattening. Paper [15] discusses securing Bloom filters by modifying bit patterns to resist attacks. None of the prior papers specifically describe XOR-composing SimHash bits to flatten the collision probability curve toward 0.5 for non-neighbors as a privacy mechanism. Paper [8] covers AND-composition for amplification but not XOR-composition for privacy/flattening.

The evaluation design involves measuring collision probability curves as a function of similarity and k, plus an ablation comparing XOR composition vs. reduced bit count. Paper [11] also performs "probabilistic analysis" of collision probability for LSH. The ablation design (swap a component, measure collision probability) is a generic experimental shape, but the collision-probability-curve evaluation is a named design present in [8] and [11].

This domain is privacy-preserving similarity search, which is directly addressed by papers [1], [2], [3], [4], [6]. Paper [1] is literally "Privacy-Preserving Similarity Search Scheme over Encrypted Word Embeddings" — same domain including text embeddings specifically.
